input.command: ls -R src; cat -n src/routes.ts; cat -n src/store.ts
input.description: List source files and show routes and store

input.command: grep -rn "deleteRepo\|'system'\|\"system\"\|isAdmin\|buildRoutes" --include=*.ts . | grep -v node_modules; ls -a; ls test tests 2>/dev/null
input.description: Search for callers, system owner references, and tests

input.command: cat -n src/api.ts | head -80; grep -rn "user\|oid" src --include=*.ts | grep -v "^src/store.ts\|^src/routes.ts" | head -30; cat package.json
input.description: Inspect API wiring and how user context is set

input.reason: I read src/routes.ts and src/store.ts. In src/store.ts:29, the SQL for a non-admin delete is `WHERE id = ? AND (owner = ? OR owner = 'system')`, so a non-admin can delete any row whose owner is 'system'. The route handler at src/routes.ts:26-33 passes `req.user` straight to `store.deleteRepo` and does no authorization of its own. I found no middleware, other caller, or test that blocks this. The only callers of deleteRepo are the route and the store, and the repository has no test files. Both findings hold.
input.summary: Non-admin repo delete filter also matches system-owned repos

findings.text: The delete route applies no ownership check of its own and relies on `Store.deleteRepo`, whose filter lets a non-admin delete system-owned repositories.
findings.reason: Claim 1, that the route has no ownership check of its own: the deleteRepo handler at src/routes.ts:26-33 only wraps `await store.deleteRepo(req.params.id, req.user);` in a try/catch that maps errors to 404. It never compares the repo owner with req.user. Claim 2, that it relies on Store.deleteRepo: line 28 passes the whole user context to the store method. Claim 3, that the store's filter lets a non-admin delete system-owned repos: the non-admin branch at src/store.ts:29 runs `DELETE FROM repos WHERE id = ? AND (owner = ? OR owner = 'system')`, which matches rows owned by 'system' whatever ctx.oid is.

findings.text: For a non-admin caller the delete also matches rows whose owner is `system`, so any authenticated user can delete shared system repositories.
findings.reason: Claim 1, that for a non-admin caller the delete also matches owner = 'system' rows: when ctx.isAdmin is false, src/store.ts:25-28 is skipped and line 29 runs `DELETE FROM repos WHERE id = ? AND (owner = ? OR owner = 'system')`. The OR clause matches system-owned rows on its own. Claim 2, that any authenticated user can delete system repos: the route at src/routes.ts:28 hands any req.user to this method with no extra check. The only condition is that the user is not an admin, and admins can already delete everything through line 26. So every user context can delete a system-owned repo by id, and the call returns 204.

input.severity_reason: This is an exploitable broken-access-control flaw. Any non-admin user can permanently delete system-owned repository records by id through the normal delete route, which means data loss of shared resources. Nothing else in the code blocks it.
